summary.text: A microscope is a laboratory instrument used to examine objects too small to be seen with the naked eye.
The most common type, and the first invented, is the optical microscope, which uses lenses to bend visible light passing through or reflecting off a sample.
Other major types include fluorescence microscopes, electron microscopes and scanning probe microscopes.

options.label: An objective lens near the specimen and an eyepiece
A mirror near the eye and a lens near the lamp
Two eyepieces facing each other
A flat glass plate and a needle mount

items.explain: Compound microscopes combine an objective lens near the specimen with an eyepiece to view a real image.

items.prompt: Early microscopes gave dim, uneven views with poor contrast. What did Kohler illumination add?

options.label: A stronger lamp that made the specimen glow
Even lighting that overcame limited contrast and resolution
A second lens that doubled the magnification
A beam of electrons in place of light

items.explain: It gives even lighting and overcomes the limited contrast and resolution of early illumination methods.

items.prompt: A biologist wants to see a clear, transparent cell without staining it. Which developments made that possible?

options.label: Larger glass globule lenses on a stand
Adjustable needle mounts held with screws
Phase contrast and differential interference contrast
Brighter electric lamps as light sources

items.explain: Phase contrast and differential interference contrast illumination allow imaging of unstained, transparent samples.

items.prompt: What was unusual about Antonie van Leeuwenhoek's microscope?

options.label: It used a single tiny ball lens yet reached high magnification
It chained many lenses together in a long tube
It used a beam of electrons to light the specimen
It used a concave mirror to light the specimen

items.explain: He reached up to 300 times magnification with a simple single lens, a very small glass ball held between metal plates.

paragraphs.heading: Seeing the very small
paragraphs.text: A microscope is a tool for looking at things too tiny for the unaided eye. The study of small objects and structures with such a tool is called microscopy. Something is called microscopic when you cannot see it at all without a microscope's help.

paragraphs.heading: Many kinds of microscope
paragraphs.text: Microscopes come in many types, and one way to sort them is by how they make an image. Some send a beam of light or electrons through or onto the sample. Others pick up light given off by the sample, and others drag a fine probe across its surface from very close by. The most common type, and the oldest, is the optical microscope: its lenses bend visible light that has passed through a thin slice of the sample, or light bounced off an object, to form an image. Other major types are the fluorescence microscope, the electron microscope and a family called scanning probe microscopes.

paragraphs.heading: From eyeglasses to the compound lens
paragraphs.text: Simple microscopes, which are just magnifying glasses, first appear in use in the 13th century, when lenses for eyeglasses became common. Compound microscopes pair an objective lens near the specimen with an eyepiece, and the earliest known ones turned up in Europe around 1620. Nobody knows who made the first one, despite many claims. The name came in 1625, when Giovanni Faber called Galileo's instrument a microscopio; Galileo himself had called it the occhiolino, or little eye.

paragraphs.heading: Opening up biology
paragraphs.text: The microscope was still mostly a novelty at first. Then, in the 1660s and 1670s, naturalists in England, Italy and the Netherlands turned it on living things. Robert Hooke's book Micrographia, published in 1665, made a big splash, mostly thanks to its striking drawings. Antonie van Leeuwenhoek reached magnifications of up to 300 times with a microscope that had just one lens, a tiny glass ball held between two riveted metal plates. With it he reported micro-organisms on 9 October 1676.

paragraphs.heading: Getting the light right
paragraphs.text: How well a compound light microscope works depends on two sets of lenses used properly. The condenser focuses light onto the specimen, and the objective gathers light from it to make the image. In 1893 August Köhler worked out a way of lighting the sample, now called Köhler illumination, that gives even light and beats the poor contrast and resolution of earlier methods. Later, phase contrast in 1953 and differential interference contrast in 1955 made it possible to image clear samples without staining them.

paragraphs.heading: Beams of electrons
paragraphs.text: In 1931 Ernst Ruska and Max Knoll built the first prototype electron microscope, a transmission electron microscope, or TEM. It follows the same basic plan as a light microscope, but uses electrons in place of light and electromagnets in place of glass lenses. Using electrons gives far sharper detail. The scanning electron microscope followed in 1935, though it was not sold commercially until 1965.

paragraphs.heading: Feeling a surface with a probe
paragraphs.text: From 1981 to 1983, Gerd Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer studied quantum tunnelling at IBM in Zürich, and from that theory they built a working scanning probe microscope. Its probe comes so close to the sample's surface that electrons flow steadily between them as a current. At first the instrument was not well received, because the theory behind it was hard to follow. The atomic force microscope came in 1986, followed by a Nobel Prize in Physics for Binnig and Rohrer.
